Answer: Neither. “Bipolar disorder” is a diagnosis whose criteria change from time to time and which is applied to a range of different concerns whose nature, courses, and underlying dynamics differ. It is not just one kind of experience, so it does not have just one kind of outcome. For some, these experiences or a vulnerability to having them will be lifelong. For some, the experiences or susceptibility will not be lifelong. The diagnosis does not try to distinguish between those two basic categories of cases and anyone insisting otherwise has not not educated themselves about the scope of what is going on. This is in addition to the complexity of how the way we respond to the experiences and causes can shape what happens on an individual basis. Can the symptoms eventually go away? Well, the first thing to address there is that these aren’t “symptoms” in the medical sense — they aren’t experiences resulting from an underlying medical condition. “Bipolar disorder” is not causing anything, it is the label some clinicians will use to refer to the experiences themselves. The cause is not commented on, and the so-called “disorder” is the experiences themselves rather than why they are happening. So, there is very much a reason for the experiences, but “bipolar disorder” neither is the reason nor does it explain the reason. It is essentially an industry shorthand for saying “those things the patient talked about with me”. The reason for these experiences will depend on the person and circumstances. “Bipolar disorder” can refer to any number of reasons. In theory, the diagnosis does not apply to experiences resulting from medical disorders or drug effects, but in reality practitioners will misdiagnose medical problems and drug reactions as “bipolar disorder” with great frequency so the diagnostic criteria and guidelines attached to them aren’t something we can rely on to describe the reality of practice. Either way, we are left with a heterogeneous collection of experiences and what is going on to cause them will usually be integral to whether and how they can be abated. Causes and how they express will shape what happens when we try to improve things. Sometimes, the underlying causes can be addressed. Other times, we can’t figure out what they are or don’t have a way to ameliorate them. In both kinds of situations, there can still potentially be strategies and interventions which reduce the intensity or frequency of the experiences under diagnosis, improve social functioning or quality of life, or provide relief in some personal manner. For some people, finding a good approach can help resolve current concerns and then entirely prevent new instances. For some people, new instances will still occur to some degree no matter what is tried. An absence of new instances does not mean vulnerabilities to recurrence are also absent, but occasionally that is the case.

Question: St. John’s Wort makes me awfully tired and unfocused. I have elevated renin which means more angiotensin 2 which raises serotonin, which induces glutamate excess. Is it the wrong medication as an SSRI?
Answer: Right/wrong is based on how you feel. The downstream effects of particular influences can be useful in some instances of troubleshooting, but none of that explains someone’s response to a drug with respect to ideas like depression because they are broad and encompassing psychosocial concepts with no specific or discrete physical underpinnings. There are no physical details you could share which would tell us whether a particular drug will feel alleviatory unless you whittle things down to specific symptoms. If feeling tired means a more stimulating drug would be appreciated, for example, that is more feasible to tailor drug use around. But that, too, is based on how you’re feeling, not things like extrapolations about glutamate. What works is what works. So, the thing to consider here is whether St John’s Wort is doing what you want it to, and whether what you want it to do is something reasonable to expect of drug use in general. If there are downsides you don’t feel worth it or there aren’t the upsides you are depending on a drug to provide, clearly it either isn’t the drug for you or is being managed inadequately. (With herbal supplements, there is also the elevated need to consider the consistency of the source — the ingredient ratio, purity, uniformity, etc.) If St John’s Wort isn’t working out for you, then maybe something else would. Maybe not, but either way, you’d have your answer as to whether this specific regimen is fitting. Dealing with whatever is causing your elevated plasma renin may be essential here, though, and make suggestions about what drugs to use. You never mention what your symptoms or treatment goals are, so what potential relevance hypericum perforatum might have is unclear. But, since PRA changes are associated with a range of medical conditions and the nature of those conditions can influence what kinds of concerns you might have and how they respond to drug use, I recommend looking at the bigger picture with your consulting clinicians in order to decipher what kind of drugging might be appropriate. It isn’t unusual for someone to find reuptake inhibitors to cause tiredness or poor focus, but whatever is going on medically needs to be accounted for as well.

Name: Mark Dunn
Question: I went from 15mg of Lexapro to 10mg in a week and now have anxiety. Is this normal?
Answer: Yes, that is very normal. There are three main reasons why patients very often experience anxiety when changing SSRI doses. The first is that these are neurodisruptive drugs and their influences will very commonly cause anxiety and other such effects when a new dose is started. Initiating a drug, increasing the dose, or reducing the dose can all be destabilizing. People usually adjust within days or weeks if this is the cause. If you notice things getting worse rather than better, it is more likely that either the anxiety is due to another drug cause or that it will not be resolving if you keep using the drug. Another primary reason for anxiety with a dose reduction is withdrawal syndrome. If someone has been using an SSRI continuously for several weeks or longer, withdrawal syndrome is to be expected and can sometimes happen even with a partial dose reduction instead of a full discontinuation of the drug. 15mg to 10mg is a significant drop and liable to cause withdrawal for many people. It may take weeks, months, or even longer to resolve, but reinstating the original dose will often help within a few days to a few weeks. Tapering more slowly may help reduce the intensity and longevity of the emergent anxiety. A third key reason why some patients experience anxiety with SSRI reduction or cessation is rebound syndrome. Though withdrawal will sometimes involve rebound symptoms, rebound can happen even if classic withdrawal does not. “Rebound” in this sense is not referring to a recurrence of previous psychological experiences, it is referring to supersensitivity in the nervous system caused by changes meant to be adaptations to drug actions. Essentially, the anxiety results from overcompensation following a dose reduction. It often takes months or years for the anxiety to fully fade.

Question: Do SSRIs have the potential to cause nerve damage?
Answer: Of course. SSRIs are neurotoxins at clinically prescribed doses, and below, so SSRIs cause neurotoxic effects. Not everyone will experience the same damages, severity or scope of damages, or symptoms as a result of damages, but these drugs have a very clear potential to cause nerve damage. Even in the information about drugs like SSRIs that pharmaceutical companies supply to the public in their pamphlets, nerve damage is usually mentioned very specifically, usually in the form of neuropathy and related terms. This is on top of the damages which can occur as a consequence of more sweeping adverse effects typically also warned about, like seizures, toxidromes, brain bleeds, or rarer effects like rhabdomyolysis, SJS/TEN. It is baffling that so many posters claiming to be professionals or knowledgeable about psychiatry are so totally oblivious to this established risk and sometimes even go so far as to try and explain it away as being the fault of patients if problems do occur. Given that the drug manufacturers themselves warn about effects which can cause nerve damage or effects which indicate nerve damage, there is no way to honestly defend SSRIs as being free of this risk. Such answers might as well be claiming that SSRIs also don’t cause impotence or apathy or serotonin syndrome either. It is ludicrous, and a scary showing of the dangerous quality of mainstream information on these drugs. There is plenty of room to debate how pervasive or how serious certain toxic influences are, or how often particular outcomes happen. Even whether particular symptoms are the result of damage rather than other drug alterations. There is a lot we still don’t know, and the mechanisms and prevalence of what we do see occurring are themselves still often at least partially unknown. In short, most of what we need studied is not given much attention and there is not much funding invested into clarifying these things because most research is oriented around marketing drugs more profitably. However, the issue of whether these drugs can cause nerve damage has been definitively settled and anyone claiming otherwise is dramatically unqualified to answer this question.

Question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have the same effect on everyone?
Answer: They have the same actions, but the result depends on the person. Drugs defined by a specific formula will have the same basic actions universally, since those actions arise from the makeup of the chemicals. But, the experienced effects of a drug like an SSRI depends on all the personal and situational factors involved as well: how someone metabolizes it, what their health is like, how their nervous system is functioning, how high their dose is and how long they take it for, and so on. Most mechanisms of SSRIs will always be in action, such as the eponymous serotonin reuptake inhibition. What that causes to happen in someone’s mind, body, or behavior is much more complex because more than just the drug action is involved. Some effects are so common that the majority of patients will experience them, even if we choose patients at random or give the drugs to random people who aren’t patients and have no reason to take them. Some effects are common but only developing in a minority of patients, often due to differences between people that only become relevant to their everyday lives in certain kinds of situations. Some effects are common but easily prevented, resulting from things like poor drug management. Many effects are less common, or outright rare, and we don’t always know why they occur. Context, management, and personal traits all play a part in drug reactions. So, SSRIs have the same fundamental effects in everyone on the pharmacological level, but what this means for someone’s experiences is more complicated and personal. Some drug effects are pretty much universal, like attenuating certain kinds of signaling and sensation, though the intensity of those effects will still vary. Some drug effects are so rare they only occur once in every 1,000 to 10,000 patients. Most effects fall between those two extremes of incidence. The most relevant thing to understand is how the mechanisms of SSRIs carry particular risks and that even if we can’t predict every outcome, we can know that there are dangers to use which must be addressed.
